    In plain words

    GitLab has released fixes for a serious flaw that could let anyone without an account read sensitive files, such as passwords, secret keys, or other private information, from affected GitLab servers. Organizations that run their own GitLab Community or Enterprise servers are affected and should update to the fixed versions immediately; GitLab.com has already been updated. Security researchers are already seeing people search online for unpatched servers, so delayed updates could expose company code and credentials to theft.

    Summary
    GitLab is urging self-managed users to immediately upgrade to versions 19.3.2, 19.2.6, or 19.1 to fix CVE-2026-85706, a maximum-severity unauthenticated path traversal flaw that can expose arbitrary server files. Internet-wide probing has already begun, making rapid patching and log review essential.

    GitLab urged users to immediately patch CVE-2026-85706, a maximum-severity path traversal issue in the repository commits API. Under certain conditions, an unauthenticated attacker can use the flaw to read arbitrary data from a vulnerable server, including credentials, secrets, and other sensitive information. watchTowr reported seeing probes for unpatched, Internet-exposed GitLab servers only a day after disclosure.

    GitLab fixed the issue in Community Edition and Enterprise Edition versions 19.3.2, 19.2.6, and 19.1, and said GitLab.com is already patched while GitLab Dedicated customers need take no action. watchTowr advised defenders to look for HTTP POST requests to /api/v4/projects/{id}/repository/commits/ addresses containing file.path parameters as potential signs of attempted abuse. The same patch release also fixed CVE-2026-87719, a critical GitLab EE issue that could allow authenticated users with Duo Chat access to steal sensitive credentials and Advanced Search instance configurations.

    • The flaw can be targeted in a single HTTP request without authentication, which means an exposed unpatched GitLab server could be probed without the attacker first obtaining an account.
    • watchTowr provided a concrete detection lead: defenders can review logs for HTTP POST requests to repository commits API URLs containing a "file.path" parameter.
    • GitLab’s September patch release addressed two distinct critical issues with different access requirements: CVE-2026-85706 can affect unauthenticated users, while CVE-2026-87719 requires an authenticated user with Duo Chat access.
    • GitLab has a history of high-impact flaws being exploited in attacks, with CISA having listed four GitLab vulnerabilities as exploited since November 2021.
    Key Points
    • 01GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706, a maximum-severity path traversal flaw in its repository commits API that can let unauthenticated attackers read arbitrary data from vulnerable servers under certain conditions.
    • 02GitLab released fixes in Community Edition and Enterprise Edition versions 19.3.2, 19.2.6, and 19.1, and urged self-managed customers to upgrade immediately.
    • 03GitLab.com is already running a patched version, and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action.
    • 04watchTowr reported observing in-the-wild probes for CVE-2026-85706 against Internet-exposed GitLab servers.
    • 05The same release also fixed CVE-2026-87719, a critical insecure deserialization issue affecting GitLab EE that could allow authenticated users with Duo Chat access to steal sensitive credentials and Advanced Search instance configurations.

In plain words

GitLab fixed a severe flaw that could let an outsider read files from a GitLab server without logging in, and attackers began checking for vulnerable servers shortly after the problem became public. It affects certain recent versions of the self-managed GitLab software used by organizations to store code and run software-building processes. Stolen files could reveal passwords, secret keys, and source code, potentially allowing attackers to tamper with software that organizations create and distribute. Organizations should install GitLab’s updated versions quickly or limit public access to their GitLab servers.

Summary
GitLab has patched CVE-2026-85706, a CVSS 10 unauthenticated path-traversal flaw in its repository commits API that can expose arbitrary server files and is already being probed in the wild. Self-managed GitLab instances should urgently upgrade to 19.3.2, 19.2.6, or 19.1.8, or restrict public access.

GitLab released patches for CVE-2026-85706, a maximum-severity CVSS 10.0 flaw in its repository commits API. The issue results from improper path restrictions and missing login checks, potentially allowing an unauthenticated user to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server under certain conditions. It affects GitLab CE and EE versions from 18.7 before 19.1.8, 19.2 before 19.2.6, and 19.3 before 19.3.2.

watchTowr said it observed active probes for the flaw beginning at 06:00 UTC on September 11, 2026, within hours of its public disclosure. Attackers could use the issue to access logs and GitLab configuration files that may contain credentials, secrets, and other sensitive information; exploitation requires at least one public project to exist. GitLab also patched CVE-2026-87719, a CVSS 9.9 GitLab EE insecure deserialization issue affecting authenticated users with Duo Chat access, and organizations with internet-exposed self-managed instances are urged to patch quickly or restrict public access.

  • Exploitation of CVE-2026-85706 requires only that at least one public project exists, lowering the barrier for attackers targeting exposed GitLab instances.
  • Defenders can look for possible exploitation attempts by reviewing logs for HTTP POST requests to /api/v4/projects/{id}/repository/commits/ that contain file.Path parameters.
  • The file-reading flaw may expose GitLab-specific configuration files and logs, creating a route to credentials, secrets, source code, and potentially software build pipelines.
  • GitLab’s patch release also addresses a separate critical GitLab EE issue affecting authenticated users with Duo Chat access, showing that organizations may need to account for more than one high-severity issue in the same updates.
Key Points
  • 01GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706, a CVSS 10.0 path traversal flaw in the repository commits API that can allow unauthenticated users to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server under certain conditions.
  • 02CVE-2026-85706 affects GitLab CE and EE versions from 18.7 before 19.1.8, 19.2 before 19.2.6, and 19.3 before 19.3.2.
  • 03watchTowr reported observing active in-the-wild probes for CVE-2026-85706 from 06:00 UTC on September 11, 2026.
  • 04GitLab also fixed CVE-2026-87719, a CVSS 9.9 insecure deserialization issue in GitLab EE that could let authenticated Duo Chat users access Advanced Search configuration and sensitive credentials.
  • 05Organizations with internet-exposed self-managed GitLab instances are urged to apply the patches promptly or limit public access, and to review logs for relevant HTTP POST requests.

thehackernews.com · 11 Sep 2026 06:19 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGScisaciscocredential-harvestingcve-2026-20079cyclops-blinkjsp-web-shellliving-off-the-landnetcatqilinreverse-shellsandwormuat-11823uat-11988uat-12197united-states

In plain words

Cisco says three groups have been using two flaws in its Secure Firewall Management Center software to break into organizations’ systems without proper permission. The affected organizations could have passwords and other sensitive information stolen, while attackers may install hidden access tools, disrupt security software, or lock selected computers and demand money through Qilin ransomware. Cisco has released fixes and urges customers using the affected software to install them quickly; U.S. federal civilian agencies are required to do so by September 12, 2026.

Summary
Cisco warns that ransomware and state-linked threat clusters are actively exploiting two patched Secure Firewall Management Center flaws to gain access, steal credentials, deploy backdoors, and in one case launch Qilin ransomware. Organizations should immediately apply Cisco’s hotfixes for CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316.

Cisco disclosed that three threat clusters linked to ransomware and state-sponsored activity have exploited two recently patched vulnerabilities in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC). CVE-2026-20079, rated 10.0, allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass web-interface authentication, execute scripts, and obtain root access to the underlying operating system. CVE-2026-20316, rated 5.3, allows unauthenticated remote login through a low-privilege account and can be combined with other FMC flaws to elevate privileges.

UAT-12197 used the critical flaw to install JSP web shells and a Java-based command tool to query internal databases and obtain authentication data and credentials. UAT-11823 exploited both flaws to deploy a Netcat reverse shell, harvest managed-device configurations, and install a Cyclops Blink variant previously attributed to Sandworm. UAT-11988 used CVE-2026-20316 for initial access, conducted reconnaissance and credential collection with built-in FMC tools, and deployed Qilin ransomware on selected systems. Cisco urges affected customers to apply released hotfixes, while CISA has added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and requires U.S. federal civilian agencies to patch CVE-2026-20079 by September 12, 2026.

  • The two flaws support different levels of access: CVE-2026-20079 can enable remote root-level access, while CVE-2026-20316 provides low-privilege access that can be combined with other FMC flaws to gain more control.
  • The same affected FMC platform was used for distinct attacker goals, including credential collection, harvesting managed-device configurations, deployment of a state-linked Cyclops Blink variant, and Qilin ransomware operations.
  • The Qilin-linked activity relied in part on legitimate built-in FMC tools to map the victim environment and identify systems for encryption, rather than relying only on externally introduced tools.
  • Patch urgency is reinforced by Cisco’s hotfix recommendation, its planned broader hardening release, and CISA’s requirement that U.S. federal civilian agencies remediate CVE-2026-20079 by September 12, 2026.
Key Points
  • 01Cisco reported that three threat clusters linked to ransomware and state-sponsored activity exploited two recently patched Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center vulnerabilities.
  • 02CVE-2026-20079 is a critical authentication-bypass flaw that can let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute scripts and obtain root access to the underlying operating system.
  • 03UAT-12197 used CVE-2026-20079 to deploy web shells and a Java-based command tool that queried internal databases for user authentication data and credentials.
  • 04UAT-11823 exploited both flaws to deploy a reverse shell, collect managed-device configurations, and install a Cyclops Blink variant.
  • 05UAT-11988 exploited CVE-2026-20316, used built-in FMC tools for reconnaissance and credential collection, and deployed Qilin ransomware on selected systems.

    In plain words

    Attackers are using weaknesses in self-hosted JFrog Artifactory servers to get around login protections, give themselves full administrator control, and install a hidden backdoor that lets them return later. They have also stolen configuration information, listed users and stored software packages, and added their own remote-login keys. This affects organizations running exposed Artifactory servers, with Wiz estimating that 49% to 62% of reachable systems may be vulnerable. Organizations should install the available updates quickly and check for unknown administrator accounts, access keys, and suspicious add-ons.

    Summary
    Attackers are actively chaining critical JFrog Artifactory flaws to bypass authentication, obtain administrator access, and deploy persistent Rust backdoors on self-hosted servers. Administrators should urgently upgrade to patched releases and investigate for rogue accounts, tokens, plugins, and other indicators of compromise.

    Threat actors are actively exploiting critical and high-severity flaws in self-hosted JFrog Artifactory servers to bypass authentication, obtain administrator privileges, and deploy a Rust-based backdoor. Wiz observed multiple actors chaining CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016 between August 15 and September 8, 2026. A third issue, CVE-2026-82329, was previously observed being exploited to create administrator tokens.

    The observed chain lets attackers obtain a low-privilege JSON Web Token for Artifactory’s internal anonymous user, even where anonymous access is disabled, then exchange it for an administrator-scoped token because of insufficient token validation. In some cases, attackers created an administrator account in under five minutes, generated long-lived tokens, installed malicious Groovy plugins for command execution, and added a Rust backdoor for persistent remote control. They also uploaded webshells, stole configuration data and cluster join keys, enumerated repositories, tokens, and users, and added SSH keys to new accounts.

    Wiz estimates that 49% to 62% of reachable Artifactory instances are vulnerable to at least one of the three flaws. Administrators are advised to upgrade to one of the listed patched Artifactory releases or later, investigate exposed instances for suspicious accounts, tokens, plugins, and enumeration activity, and restrict access to trusted systems. Wiz also published indicators of compromise associated with the observed attacks.

    • Disabling anonymous access did not prevent attackers from obtaining a token for Artifactory’s internal anonymous user through CVE-2026-42018.
    • In some observed cases, attackers needed less than five minutes to create an administrator account after targeting a vulnerable instance.
    • The attackers established persistence through both long-lived access tokens and malicious Groovy plugins, rather than relying only on a single backdoor.
    • Artifactory cluster join keys and configuration data were among the information stolen, alongside repository, token, and user enumeration.
    Key Points
    • 01Multiple threat actors exploited CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016 against self-hosted JFrog Artifactory instances between August 15 and September 8, 2026.
    • 02The exploit chain obtains a low-privilege token for Artifactory’s internal anonymous user and then uses insufficient token validation to obtain an administrator-scoped token.
    • 03Attackers created administrator accounts, generated long-lived access tokens, installed malicious Groovy plugins, and deployed a Rust-based backdoor with command-and-control capabilities.
    • 04The attackers also downloaded payloads to temporary directories, uploaded webshells, stole Artifactory configuration data and cluster join keys, and enumerated repositories, tokens, and users.
    • 05Wiz estimates that 49% to 62% of reachable Artifactory instances are vulnerable to at least one of the three identified flaws and recommends upgrading to patched releases.

In plain words

Attackers have been breaking into unpatched self-hosted JFrog Artifactory servers, which companies use to store software components for their build systems, and giving themselves full administrator control. They used flaws that let them obtain access without logging in, create hidden administrator accounts, and install programs that let them continue controlling the server. This matters because a compromised software repository can affect the systems and software that depend on it, and simply installing the updates may not remove accounts, access keys, or backdoors already planted.

Summary
Attackers are actively chaining two patched JFrog Artifactory flaws, CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016, to obtain administrator access and deploy persistent backdoors on unpatched self-hosted servers. Organizations should urgently upgrade, rotate join keys and tokens, and investigate for rogue admin accounts, plugins, and activity attributed to token:anonymous.

Wiz observed attackers exploiting unpatched self-hosted JFrog Artifactory servers between August 15 and September 8 by chaining CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016. The first flaw can provide an internal anonymous-user token to someone who has not logged in, while the second can let that low-privilege token be exchanged for one with administrator scope. Actions performed with the resulting token may appear in logs as token:anonymous, despite having administrator-level permissions. Wiz saw some attackers create new administrator accounts in less than five minutes.

With administrator access, attackers created persistent administrator accounts, installed malicious Groovy plugins that enabled code execution on the server, and ran shell commands to explore files. A dropper downloaded a binary over HTTP into locations such as /tmp and opened a command-and-control channel, while a custom Rust backdoor was also seen in multiple cases. Separately, CVE-2026-82329 is a critical authentication bypass that can grant unauthenticated attackers administrator privileges on its own across affected Artifactory release branches. Updating Artifactory is necessary, but it does not remove accounts, tokens, backdoors, or join keys that may already have been created or stolen, so the article recommends reviewing administrator accounts and configuration changes and rotating join keys and relevant tokens.

  • Administrator actions performed through the chained flaws can appear in Artifactory logs as "token:anonymous," which can obscure that an attacker had elevated privileges.
  • Wiz observed some attackers progress from an unauthenticated request to creating a new administrator account in under five minutes.
  • Although the two-flaw chain does not affect certain newer Artifactory branches, the separate CVE-2026-82329 authentication bypass can still affect releases up to version 7.161.
  • For CVE-2026-82329, organizations unable to upgrade immediately can add a randomly generated extra join key in system.yaml so only their own keys are accepted during service registration.
  • Fastly recorded roughly 406,000 CVE-2026-82329 exploitation attempts on September 2, but noted that these traffic observations do not represent confirmed compromises.
Key Points
  • 01Wiz observed attacks from August 15 to September 8 that chained CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016 in unpatched self-hosted JFrog Artifactory servers to obtain administrator-level access.
  • 02CVE-2026-42018 can return an internal anonymous-user token to an unauthenticated caller, while CVE-2026-42016 can allow a low-privilege token to be exchanged for one with administrator scope.
  • 03Attackers created administrator accounts, installed malicious Groovy plugins for server code execution, ran shell commands, and in some cases deployed a custom Rust backdoor.
  • 04CVE-2026-82329 is a separate critical authentication bypass that can grant unauthenticated attackers administrator privileges on affected Artifactory branches without requiring another flaw.
  • 05Patching does not remove administrator accounts, tokens, backdoors, or join keys that attackers may have already created or stolen, so affected organizations should also rotate join keys and tokens and review accounts and configuration changes.

JUSTIFICATION

This is an active in-the-wild exploitation report affecting self-hosted JFrog Artifactory, where attackers can obtain administrator access, establish persistence, and deploy backdoors. It includes a separate critical authentication bypass, concrete fixed versions, and post-compromise actions because patching alone does not remove attacker-created accounts, tokens, or stolen join keys.

In plain words

PaperCut has released tested software updates to replace earlier emergency fixes for two security problems in its PaperCut NG/MF printing-management software. Attackers are already using these problems to get around login protections and run their own commands on affected systems, with one campaign reaching at least 395 organizations in 48 countries, especially U.S. schools. Installing the latest updates matters because stolen access could later be used for goals such as taking data or deploying ransomware.

Summary
PaperCut has released fully tested maintenance updates for PaperCut NG/MF that replace emergency patches for CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, two actively exploited flaws enabling authentication bypass and arbitrary code execution. Organizations should upgrade to versions 26.0.5, 25.0.13, or 24.1.10 immediately.

PaperCut released regular maintenance updates for PaperCut NG/MF that replace all previously issued emergency patches for two actively exploited security flaws. The available versions are 26.0.5, 25.0.13, and 24.1.10. PaperCut said the releases include fixes from Emergency Patch Releases 1, 2, and 3, additional security hardening, and complete quality-assurance and standard release testing.

The flaws, CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078, have been exploited to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary code on affected instances. GreyNoise and Blackpoint Cyber reported that a suspected Russian-speaking actor used the flaws to break into at least 395 organizations in 48 countries, with many targets in the U.S. education sector. The activity reportedly used hundreds of AI agents powered by OpenAI’s Codex harness and a DeepSeek model, and PaperCut advises customers on emergency-patch builds to move to the latest maintenance releases.

  • Organizations that installed PaperCut’s earlier emergency patches are still advised to upgrade, because the new maintenance releases supersede those builds and add further security hardening.
  • The reported campaign used hundreds of AI agents powered by OpenAI’s Codex harness and a DeepSeek model, illustrating that the actors conducted activity at scale across 48 countries.
  • The suspected actor reportedly avoided targets in Russia, China, Hong Kong, Thailand, Iran, and 23 additional countries, while concentrating many compromises in the U.S. education sector.
  • GreyNoise stated that it remains unclear whether the actor is only obtaining access for other actors or intends to use it directly for data theft or ransomware deployment.
Key Points
  • 01PaperCut released regular maintenance versions 26.0.5, 25.0.13, and 24.1.10 for PaperCut NG/MF, replacing its previous emergency patches.
  • 02The maintenance releases include the fixes from Emergency Patch Releases 1, 2, and 3, along with additional security hardening and standard quality-assurance testing.
  • 03CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 are being actively exploited to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary code on vulnerable PaperCut instances.
  • 04GreyNoise and Blackpoint Cyber reported that a suspected Russian-speaking actor used the two flaws to compromise at least 395 organizations in 48 countries, with many targets in the U.S. education sector.
  • 05PaperCut advises customers using an emergency patch build to move to a regular maintenance release.

    In plain words

    Anthropic says it stopped a Russia-linked spy group from using its Claude AI tool while targeting Ukrainian government, military, diplomatic, and drone-related organizations. The group reportedly broke into email accounts, stole drone software, and used AI to understand it and adjust its digital tools when security software spotted them. The report also found criminal groups, Chinese-speaking operators, and a French-speaking activist using AI in harmful online activity. This matters because AI can help smaller or less-skilled groups carry out complex digital break-ins faster, potentially making it harder for organizations and governments to keep up.

    Summary
    Anthropic says it disrupted Russia-linked Midnight Blizzard operators who used Claude to support cyber-espionage against Ukrainian and defense-related targets, including reverse-engineering stolen drone software and adapting tools to evade detections. The report also describes AI misuse by criminal, Chinese-speaking, and hacktivist actors, underscoring how AI can accelerate sophisticated cyber operations.

    Anthropic said it detected and disrupted a Russia-linked cyber-espionage campaign that used Claude against more than 20 government, intelligence, diplomatic, and defense organizations between December 2025 and August 2026. The company said the activity aligned with Midnight Blizzard, also known as APT29 and Cozy Bear, which Western intelligence agencies attribute to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. The targets included Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic personnel, as well as entities in the drone supply chain.

    The operators allegedly compromised hotel Wi-Fi providers, altered DNS records to redirect travelers to attacker-controlled infrastructure, and accessed mailboxes at two drone-component manufacturers. Anthropic said they then stole a military drone maker’s proprietary vision-system software development kit and used Claude to recover product architecture, hardware components, supplier dependencies, and details of an unannounced product. The group also reportedly used Claude to modify and redeploy tools after security products detected them, while Anthropic warned that AI can help capable attackers adapt faster and reduce the expertise needed for complex campaigns.

    • The reported use of Claude to modify and redeploy tools after security products detected them suggests AI can help attackers respond to new defenses faster than defenders can update and distribute detections.
    • The campaign’s focus on drone-control and AI-vision firmware shows that stolen software can be used to reveal product architecture, hardware components, suppliers, and even details of products not yet announced.
    • Anthropic’s examples indicate that AI-assisted cyber activity is not limited to state-linked groups: suspected criminals, university students, and a hacktivist also used Claude for complex operations.
    • Despite the AI use, the report says successful intrusions still depended on established entry methods such as phishing, stolen credentials, exposed services, and software flaws.
    • Anthropic published technical campaign details and indicators that security teams can use, while the article notes that the report does not provide broader figures on the overall scale of detected misuse.

    • 02Anthropic assessed the activity aligned with Midnight Blizzard, a group attributed by Western intelligence agencies to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, and said it repeatedly targeted Ukrainian government, military, diplomatic personnel, and organizations in the drone supply chain.

    • 05The report also described Claude misuse by suspected ShinyHunters affiliates, a Chinese-speaking group researching zero-day flaws in a major security product, and a French-speaking hacktivist targeting European political parties, media organizations, and think tanks.

The group targeted government, military, diplomatic, and defense-related organizations, especially in Ukraine and Europe, and also used compromised hotel Wi-Fi systems to identify and target guests. This matters because AI may let attackers adapt more quickly, making it harder for organizations to block harmful software and protect sensitive communications, identity records, emails, and live camera feeds.

Summary
Anthropic says a Russian state-linked group associated with Midnight Blizzard used Claude to automate malware rebuilding and redeployment whenever security tools detected it, accelerating evasion efforts. The campaign targeted government, defense, diplomatic, and related organizations across Ukraine, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia using phishing, DNS hijacking, credential theft, and tailored mobile and Windows malware.

Anthropic said it disrupted an AI-assisted campaign by GTG-20006, a Russian state-sponsored espionage group it associates with Midnight Blizzard, also known as APT29 or Cozy Bear. The group targeted military intelligence, government, diplomatic, defense, and related organizations, principally in Ukraine and Europe, with additional targets in the Middle East and Asia. Anthropic said the actor used Claude throughout its operations, including to register domains, establish phishing infrastructure, and monitor command-and-control channels.

A central feature of the campaign was an automated process that monitored whether deployed malware had been detected and then modified and rebuilt it to bypass those detections. The actor used phishing, ClickFix lures, and compromised hotel guest Wi-Fi vendors to redirect victims toward attacker-controlled services, delivering malware tailored for Windows, Android, and iOS devices. The campaign also included Microsoft 365 token theft, credential stealing, WhatsApp account takeovers, access to live camera streams, and the theft of identity, commercial registry, email, and other sensitive records.

  • The group’s AI-assisted workflow was designed not only to create malicious tools but to watch for detection and autonomously rebuild them, reducing the time defenders have to rely on static indicators.
  • Compromising hotel guest Wi-Fi vendors enabled the actor to redirect guest traffic through altered DNS records and collect device identifiers and IP addresses before serving device-specific Windows, Android, or iOS lures.
  • The campaign used information taken from hotel management systems and guest devices to identify additional people of interest, including Ukrainian government officials and drone manufacturers.
  • The actor reportedly used headless browsers to link victims’ WhatsApp accounts as companion devices, bulk-export Russian- and Ukrainian-language conversations, and suppress read receipts.
  • The group also exploited authorization flaws in camera-streaming service interfaces to enumerate users and obtain tokens for victims’ live camera streams.

In plain words

A China-linked hacking group used a weakness in the Windows version of Sogou Input Method, a Chinese typing tool used by hundreds of millions of people, to install software that gave them remote control of a victim’s computer. Someone could be led to a harmful link through email or chat, and the program’s outdated built-in web browser allowed the attackers to run programs as the signed-in user. Tencent released an update to block this route, but the article says the old browser component and some of its safety protections remain unchanged, making updates and awareness important for users who may have been exposed.

Summary
China-linked UNC3569 exploited a Sogou Input Method Windows flaw to use a single crafted link to launch an outdated, unsandboxed Chromium instance and install the GRAYRABBIT backdoor. Tencent patched the link-handler entry point in Sogou Input Method version 16.3.0.3498, but its embedded Chromium 80 engine and disabled browser protections remain.

Gen Digital said China-linked UNC3569 exploited a flaw in the Windows version of Sogou Input Method to install its GRAYRABBIT backdoor. The attack used a crafted sgbiz: link to pass attacker-controlled arguments to Sogou’s settings program, which opened an attacker-selected site in the application’s built-in browser. Gen said a victim clicking the link was enough to give the attacker code execution with the logged-in user’s privileges, although Tencent said social engineering would be needed to have the user authorize a browser pop-up.

The exploit used CVE-2021-38003, a Chrome JavaScript-engine flaw fixed in 2021 but still present in Sogou’s Chromium 80 build from 2020. Gen found that Sogou’s browser sandbox and same-origin protection were disabled, removing a normal barrier between a compromised web page and the computer. The payload used a malicious DLL loaded through 7-Zip to install GRAYRABBIT, which provides remote command access and communicates over RC4-scrambled TCP on port 443.

Tencent released a fix in Sogou Input Method version 16.3.0.3498 that blocks unapproved web addresses in the sgbiz: link handler. However, Gen found that the product still uses Chromium 80 and retains the disabled browser security settings. The article advises updating Sogou Input Method and checking for published indicators, including files written to C:\Users\Public\Documents and connections to mail.uaiubifas[.]top.

  • Tencent’s patch restricts the web addresses accepted by the Sogou link handler, but Gen found that the product still uses Chromium 80 with its sandbox and web-security protections disabled.
  • The malicious loader avoided many automated analysis environments by decrypting its payload only when it detected at least 50 running processes, then removed itself using an NTFS alternate data stream.
  • Even though the backdoor used port 443, its communications were RC4-scrambled plain TCP rather than normal TLS-encrypted web traffic, providing a specific detection clue.
  • The affected input method has a very large potential reach: Citizen Lab estimated more than 455 million monthly users across Windows, Android, and iOS, although Gen’s reported flaw is in the Windows version.
Key Points
  • 01Gen Digital reported that China-linked UNC3569 exploited a flaw in the Windows version of Sogou Input Method to deploy the GRAYRABBIT backdoor.
  • 02A crafted sgbiz: link could pass attacker-controlled arguments to Sogou's settings program, which opened the attacker’s chosen website in its built-in browser.
  • 03The attack used CVE-2021-38003 in Sogou’s Chromium 80-based browser, whose sandbox and same-origin protections were disabled, to run code with the logged-in user’s privileges.
  • 04The attackers used a malicious DLL loaded by 7-Zip to decrypt and install GRAYRABBIT, which communicates with mail.uaiubifas[.]top over RC4-scrambled TCP traffic on port 443.
  • 05Tencent patched the link handler in Sogou Input Method version 16.3.0.3498, but Gen found that the embedded Chromium 80 engine and disabled browser security settings remained unchanged.

In plain words

Groups linked to ShinyHunters, Helix, and other extortion operations are pretending to be company IT help desks and telling employees they must urgently update their sign-in settings. The links or codes they provide can give criminals access to an employee’s Microsoft 365 account, even though the message may mention newer passwordless sign-in methods. Once inside, the criminals can look through company email, shared files, and online work tools, then slowly download data over hours or days to avoid notice. This puts organizations at risk of losing sensitive business information and gives attackers a way to keep accessing accounts by adding their own sign-in methods.

Summary
Microsoft warns that ShinyHunters-, Helix-, and related extortion actors are using passkey- and SSO-themed phishing to steal Microsoft 365 credentials or tokens, then map cloud environments and quietly exfiltrate SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange data. Organizations should watch for anomalous sign-ins, new MFA registrations, Graph reconnaissance, and device-code abuse.

Microsoft says threat actors linked to ShinyHunters, Helix, and other extortion groups have used passkey- and single sign-on-themed social engineering since May 2026 to compromise corporate Microsoft accounts. The actors research organizations and employees, impersonate IT help desks by phone or message, and claim that victims must urgently update passkey, MFA, or SSO settings. Victims are sent to Microsoft-lookalike phishing sites or persuaded to enter a code on Microsoft’s legitimate device authentication page. Although the lures invoke passkeys, Microsoft says the actors are not attempting to enroll passkeys.

The campaigns can capture credentials and active sessions or authorize an attacker-controlled OAuth application, allowing access to the victim’s Microsoft 365 resources and connected SSO applications. After compromise, Microsoft observed attackers examining applications, user and organizational information, privileges, authentication methods, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange content, including through Microsoft Graph. The actors may add phone numbers, authenticator apps, or software one-time-password methods to retain access, then collect cloud data gradually over hours or days, often staying below 1,000 files or emails per hour. Microsoft recommends monitoring for unusual sign-ins, new MFA registrations, Graph reconnaissance, and suspicious cloud-data access, and responding with credential and session resets plus removal of attacker-added authentication methods or mailbox rules.

  • Although the lures mention passkeys, Microsoft says the actors are not trying to enroll passkeys; they use the theme to persuade victims to sign in through credential-and-session-stealing websites or authorize attacker-controlled applications with device codes.
  • A victim who enters a supplied device code on Microsoft’s legitimate authentication page can grant an attacker-controlled OAuth application access without the attacker needing to complete another MFA challenge.
  • Routine Microsoft Graph requests such as queries for users, groups, and sites become more suspicious when the same account, application, or access token rapidly checks privileges and authentication settings before accessing mail and files.
  • The actors appear to reduce detection risk by limiting collection to fewer than 1,000 files or emails per hour and spreading theft across hours or days instead of rapidly extracting data.
  • Persistence through attacker-added MFA methods does not survive a complete credential and session reset, according to Microsoft.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft says threat actors linked to ShinyHunters, Helix, and other extortion groups have used passkey- and single sign-on-themed social engineering since May 2026 to compromise corporate Microsoft accounts.
  • 02The attackers impersonate IT help desks and direct employees to fake Microsoft sign-in pages or persuade them to enter device codes on legitimate Microsoft authentication pages.
  • 03After gaining access, the actors use Microsoft Graph and other Microsoft 365 services to identify available applications, users, privileges, email, SharePoint sites, OneDrive files, and other cloud resources.
  • 04Microsoft observed high-volume but deliberately paced downloads of SharePoint and OneDrive data, as well as some Exchange email access, with activity sometimes lasting from hours to multiple days.
  • 05The attackers may establish persistence by registering phone numbers, authenticator apps, or software-based one-time-password methods on compromised accounts.

In plain words

A browser add-on called Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot, used by about 31,000 people on Chrome and Firefox, quietly sent users’ Twitch login access keys to servers run by the service behind the add-on. Anyone holding those keys could use a person’s Twitch account without needing their password or second-factor code, including sending messages, chatting, or spending channel points. The add-on claimed it did not collect user data, so affected users should remove it and sign out of all Twitch sessions to invalidate the shared keys.

Summary
The Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot extension, installed by roughly 31,000 Chrome and Firefox users, sends live Twitch OAuth session tokens to JeetBot-controlled proxy servers, potentially allowing account takeover actions. Users should remove the extension and revoke all Twitch sessions to invalidate exposed tokens.

Socket’s Threat Research Team identified the Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot browser extension as forwarding live Twitch OAuth session tokens to proxy servers operated by JeetBot, a Russian-language commercial bot service. The extension was live on the Chrome Web Store with approximately 30,000 users and on Firefox Add-ons with 552 users at the time of writing. It advertises ad blocking, 1080p playback, region-unlocked streams, and automatic channel-point collection, while redirecting Twitch video playlist requests through operator-controlled proxies.

Current v85.x builds capture the Authorization header used by Twitch’s web client, extract the raw token, and append it as an auth query parameter to proxy redirects for every watched channel except a hardcoded list of ten Russian streamer channels. Earlier v4.x builds directly POSTed captured tokens to set-token endpoints on JeetBot infrastructure and backup Deno services. Because the account-level OAuth token can permit actions such as reading and sending whispers, posting in chat, and spending channel points without a password or second factor, the article recommends removing the extension and disconnecting all Twitch sessions to invalidate forwarded tokens.

  • The extension sends a full account-level Twitch credential even though it handles the separate video-stream token in the Twitch playback URL, exposing more account access than video delivery requires.
  • Putting the OAuth token in an auth URL parameter means it is recorded in proxy request logs in cleartext.
  • JeetBot’s server-side proxy catalog can determine which proxy host receives users’ tokens, allowing the destination to be changed through its configuration service.
  • Earlier builds used a dedicated set-token endpoint and tracked the last sent token with a five-second cooldown, while later builds switched to forwarding the token inline with proxied requests.
  • The extension’s token forwarding contradicts its Chrome Web Store data-safety statement and linked privacy policy, both of which state that it does not collect or process user data.
Key Points
  • 01Socket’s Threat Research Team found that the Twitch Enhanced Viewer | JeetBot extension forwards users’ live Twitch OAuth session tokens to proxy servers operated by JeetBot.
  • 02The extension was live on the Chrome Web Store with about 30,000 users and Firefox Add-ons with 552 users at the time of writing.
  • 03Current v85.x builds append the Twitch OAuth token as an auth query parameter when redirecting Twitch video-playlist requests through operator-controlled proxies, except for ten hardcoded Russian streamer channels.
  • 04Earlier v4.x builds POSTed captured tokens to set-token endpoints hosted by JeetBot and backup Deno services.
  • 05A holder of an exposed Twitch OAuth session token can act on the account without the password or second factor, including reading and sending whispers, posting in chat, and spending channel points.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete, active credential-exposure finding affecting roughly 31,000 Twitch users through live Chrome and Firefox extension listings. It includes actionable extension IDs, infrastructure indicators, and remediation steps, making it relevant to endpoint, browser-extension, and threat-hunting teams.

Anthropic says it disrupted large-scale unauthorized Claude distillation campaigns allegedly run by seven China-based AI labs, which used fraudulent accounts, proxy networks, and rerouted user requests to harvest Claude outputs and reasoning traces for model training.

Anthropic said it identified and disrupted industrial-scale unauthorized attempts to copy Claude’s capabilities by seven China-based AI labs, including Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek, Z.ai, Xiaomi, SenseTime, and MiniMax. The company described the activity as illicit distillation, in which a model’s outputs are collected without authorization and used to train another model. Anthropic said the campaigns sought capabilities including reasoning, tool use, coding, data analysis, and agentic tasks.

Anthropic said it has banned certain reseller and unsupported-region accounts, changed Claude to summarize internal reasoning before responding, and introduced encrypted preserved thinking to make stolen reasoning transcripts and context manipulation less useful.

  • Anthropic changed Claude to summarize its internal reasoning before answering and introduced encrypted “preserved thinking” for new API accounts, specifically to reduce the usefulness of stolen reasoning transcripts and prevent context manipulation.

In plain words

A global pharmaceutical manufacturer received emails claiming that benefit statements were ready, with a button that downloaded a Windows program from GitHub. The emails appeared trustworthy because they were sent through a real business domain and linked to a widely used legitimate platform, so normal spam and web-link checks did not stop them. This matters because criminals can use trusted services to deliver harmful files without needing an obvious fake website, putting employees and organizations at risk if someone opens the download.

Summary
A phishing campaign used a fully authenticated legitimate business domain and a GitHub release link to deliver a Windows executable, bypassing reputation-based checks because no attacker-controlled domain was involved. The key lesson is that email defenses must assess the final downloaded content and behavioral context, not just sender authentication and host reputation.

In late August 2026, a global pharmaceutical contract development and manufacturing organization received a benefits-statement phishing email with an “Obtain Statement” button linked to a Windows executable hosted as a GitHub release asset. The message passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, composite authentication, and Microsoft filtering, which assigned it a non-spam score and delivered it to the inbox. The sending domain belonged to a real U.S. business unconnected to benefits administration and used a mainstream email service provider, making that business a victim rather than an identified attacker. The campaign ultimately touched five mailboxes across four related subject lines.

The clicked GitHub URL received a Clean scanner verdict, while the redirected GitHub release-asset CDN URL received a Mixed Result verdict. No binary was retrieved, so the article does not establish the file’s hash, behavior, or malware family. Each recipient received a slightly different link because their email domain was appended as a bare query string, limiting exact-match URL blocklisting and message-hash deduplication. The article’s central finding is that sender authentication and trusted-host reputation verified legitimate infrastructure, but neither assessed the risk of an executable uploaded to that infrastructure.

  • A Clean verdict for the clicked GitHub URL reflected the reputation of the legitimate hosting platform rather than the safety of the executable it delivered.
  • The recipient’s email domain was appended as a bare query string, giving each recipient a different URL and defeating exact-match URL blocklists and message-hash deduplication without demonstrating that data was sent back to the attacker.
  • The short-lived signed CDN URL could not be rechecked minutes later because GitHub release downloads generate fresh 300-second tokens; this limitation is inherent to the platform’s delivery process rather than evidence of attacker-specific evasion.
  • Sender authentication established that the email traveled through authorized infrastructure, but it did not establish that the authenticated business intended to send the benefits-themed message.
  • The article found that detection was stronger than response: several secondary mailboxes were marked with a mitigation status but had no action taken, while another was not mitigated at all.

  • 03The URL scanner rated the GitHub link Clean, but the release-asset CDN URL reached after redirection received a Mixed Result verdict.
  • 04The executable was not retrieved, so the article does not establish its hash, behavior, or malware family.
  • 05The campaign affected five mailboxes under four related subject lines, and the article reports that several secondary mailboxes had no mitigation action taken.

Huntress recommends restricting clipboard-driven script execution, using application allow-listing, watching for new scheduled tasks and antivirus exclusions, training users to spot ClickFix-style lures, and quickly reporting suspicious AI-hosted content.

  • The attacks did not require breaking into AI platforms; they relied on users trusting legitimate platform branding and real domains.
  • Malicious AI-hosted pages can remain effective even when removed quickly, because campaigns may operate for only hours or days before takedown.
  • In the FakeAgent case, removing the malicious Claude Artifact did not immediately stop related activity because the same external redirect domain continued to be linked to incidents into August.
  • Search advertising and search-result ranking can make malicious content on trusted AI domains appear alongside legitimate troubleshooting resources, reducing common warning signs such as lookalike web addresses.
  • Monitoring for new scheduled tasks and antivirus exclusion changes can help detect the downstream behavior associated with these campaigns.
Key Points
  • 01Huntress reported that threat actors have abused shareable AI content, public mini-apps, and sponsored search results to distribute malware through trusted AI platforms over the past nine months.
  • 02In July, the FakeAgent campaign used a malicious Claude Artifact that impersonated a Claude Desktop download page and redirected victims to SectopRAT malware.
  • 03A sponsored Google result for "Claude on Mac" led victims to a fake claude.ai/share installation guide that used a curl command to deploy the MacSync stealer.
  • 04Attackers also used shared, search-optimized ChatGPT and Grok conversations to present fake macOS disk-cleanup advice that delivered the AMOS stealer.
  • 05Huntress recommends restricting clipboard-based script execution, enforcing application allow-listing, monitoring for new scheduled tasks and antivirus exclusion changes, and quickly reporting suspicious AI-hosted content.

Microsoft has fixed a bug that prevented Microsoft Teams and the new Outlook for Windows from launching, or caused them to close unexpectedly, on ARM-based Windows devices. The issue affected Windows 11 version 24H2 or later after security updates released on or after August 11, 2026, including KB5121003. Devices cited by Microsoft include the Surface Pro 11 and Surface Laptop 7.

Microsoft said the issue was most likely to affect new or freshly imaged PCs that had not installed Microsoft Store updates. Before a permanent fix was available, Microsoft advised affected users to update the Auto Super Resolution Package as a temporary workaround.

In plain words

The article explains how flaws and unsafe settings in Linux can let someone with an ordinary account gain complete control of a computer. It tests ways to spot this behavior, including suspicious programs run from temporary folders, misuse of built-in administrator tools, and sudden changes from a normal user to the system administrator account. This matters to people and organizations running Linux because a small initial foothold can become access to private files, passwords, and the ability to change the whole system.

Summary
Linux local privilege-escalation exploits increasingly reuse a small set of bug classes, but most can be detected through the common outcome of an unprivileged process or writable-path executable gaining root privileges. Elastic recommends layered detection combining root-transition and SUID/SGID behavior rules with targeted signals for namespaces, page-cache corruption, and privileged helper abuse.

Elastic presents a layered approach to detecting Linux local privilege escalation, where an attacker with a low-privilege account gains root-level control of a host. The article says the pace of disclosed Linux privilege-escalation flaws increased in 2026, with several sharing copy-on-write or zero-copy failures that can alter cached privileged files. Rather than creating a separate detection for every CVE, the framework combines detection of common escalation outcomes with rules for recurring bug classes. The common observable pattern is an unprivileged process, often launched from a writable location such as /tmp or /home, followed by a root UID change, a privileged helper execution, or an interactive root shell.

The article evaluates the framework against 11 public exploit proof-of-concepts and two SUID misconfiguration cases, including Copy Fail, DirtyFrag, DirtyDecrypt, pedit COW, DirtyClone, CIFSwitch, OVSwrap, and CVE-2026-46333 descriptor-theft examples. It describes detection signals such as suspicious SUID/SGID helper use, Python processes changing to root, unshare namespace creation followed by elevation, and risky activity involving writable paths, compilation, local networking, mounts, sudoers files, or D-Bus calls. Some exploits expose a clear technique-specific signal, such as Copy Fail’s AF_ALG socket and splice() activity, while others are detected mainly through their final privileged behavior. The article also notes that successful escalation does not always create a root shell, because attacks against CVE-2026-46333 can instead steal sensitive file descriptors containing SSH host keys or access to /etc/shadow.

  • A successful local privilege escalation may not produce a root shell: the CVE-2026-46333 examples instead steal sensitive file descriptors containing SSH host keys or access to /etc/shadow.
  • Correlating user-namespace creation with a subsequent transition to root reduces noise because legitimate sandboxing and container tools may use unshare but rarely become root in the same process lineage.
  • For quiet kernel bugs such as DirtyClone, the article found that a generic Python process changing to root from a user-controlled directory could be the only useful endpoint alert.
  • A root transition observed after namespace creation must be validated carefully, because it can represent root only inside a namespace rather than completed root access on the host.
  • The article argues that exploit-specific rules can arrive too late when one copy-on-write bug pattern is rapidly reproduced across many Linux kernel interfaces, making outcome-focused detections more durable.
Key Points
  • 01The article proposes a layered Linux local privilege-escalation detection model that combines general root-transition detection with rules tailored to recurring exploit classes.
  • 02Its general detection logic focuses on a non-root process executing from a user-writable location and then producing a root UID change, privileged helper execution, or root shell.
  • 03The article evaluates 11 public exploit proofs of concept and two SUID misconfiguration cases, covering page-cache corruption, namespace abuse, trusted-helper abuse, privileged file-descriptor theft, and SUID abuse.
  • 04Copy Fail can be detected through bursts of AF_ALG socket and splice activity as well as the later suspicious execution of a SUID/SGID helper.
  • 05The article emphasizes that outcome-oriented detection can remain useful when exploit-specific kernel activity is quiet or differs across individual CVEs.

In plain words

The article found many newly created AI-powered websites aimed at students that ask for homework photos, school records, essays, test scores, camera or microphone access, and other personal information. These sites are often built quickly with tools such as Lovable and Replit, and many show signs that their creators did not finish basic setup or provide clear privacy information. Children, families, students applying to college, and teachers may be affected because the information can reveal names, handwriting, schools, voices, screens, and personal goals. The larger concern is that easy app-building tools let people collect highly sensitive student information before they understand how to protect it or where it is stored.

Summary
Censys research finds a growing wave of AI-built student-facing apps that collect sensitive homework, academic, camera, microphone, and admissions data without clear privacy safeguards or evidence that operators understand the infrastructure handling it. The primary risk is not conventional malware but negligent data collection enabled by low-friction app-building platforms.

Censys analyzed Internet-wide scan data to identify AI-built web applications aimed at students and children, including homework helpers, GPA calculators, scholarship matchers, essay graders, and admissions predictors. The identified sites advertise collecting academic information such as homework photos, essays, test scores, transcripts, extracurricular activities, and admissions profiles. More than 75% of the population was deployed within the prior year, and Lovable accounted for roughly 229 sites compared with 45 built with Replit.

Censys found direct evidence of file uploads, camera or microphone access, or storage-related capabilities in roughly 30% of its sample, while 61% of Lovable-built sites still used default Lovable social-media branding. Most sites did not show conventional malicious indicators such as phishing kits, malware delivery, or obfuscated code, but often lacked visible privacy policies while soliciting sensitive student data. One exception, Lingua AI, ran on a host with more than 30 open ports, NPS tunneling, a DERP relay endpoint, publicly displayed demo credentials, and multiple services handling student, teacher, and administrator access.

  • The article argues that AI app-building tools have removed the former practical barrier to creating public systems that accept strangers’ data, allowing operators to deploy authentication, uploads, and storage without necessarily understanding the resulting privacy responsibilities.
  • Default Lovable social-card and favicon settings appeared on many sites collecting student information, making unfinished platform branding a visible indicator that an operator may have deployed sensitive intake features with minimal customization.
  • Conventional threat detection produced almost no malware, phishing, or other malicious signals across the population, showing that careless collection of children’s data falls outside the threat categories those tools are designed to identify.
  • The article’s three-layer search method combines student-targeting language, AI-development provenance, and evidence of upload or device-access features, allowing the population to be monitored rather than treated as a one-time set of examples.
Key Points
  • 01Censys identified a population of AI-built, student-facing web applications that advertise collecting academic information such as homework, GPAs, essays, test scores, extracurricular activities, and admissions profiles.
  • 02More than 75% of the identified population was deployed within the previous year, and Lovable accounted for roughly 229 sites compared with 45 Replit sites.
  • 03Roughly 30% of the sampled sites showed direct evidence of file uploads, camera or microphone access, or storage-related features such as Supabase or Firebase.
  • 04Sixty-one percent of the Lovable-built sites still used default Lovable social-media branding, including unmodified preview images or Lovable Twitter account metadata.
  • 05Most sites showed no conventional malicious indicators, but Lingua AI was hosted on a system with more than 30 open ports, NPS tunneling, a DERP relay endpoint, and publicly displayed default demo credentials of admin / 123qwe.

In plain words

The article argues that the most serious-looking software flaw is not always the one most likely to lead to a real break-in. A less severe flaw can be more dangerous if someone can use it as a first step, combine it with other weaknesses, and reach valuable data or powerful systems. It says organizations of all sizes need ongoing tests as their apps, cloud services, and access settings change, rather than relying only on occasional reviews or lists of flaws. BreachLock promotes its Breach360 service as a way to run these tests repeatedly, while people still decide which risks matter most to the business.

Summary
BreachLock argues that vulnerability severity alone is a poor indicator of risk; organizations should continuously validate whether weaknesses can be chained into real attack paths to sensitive assets. The company positions its Breach360 autonomous penetration-testing platform as a scalable way to provide that evidence, while retaining human judgment for remediation priorities.

The article argues that vulnerability severity scores alone do not show an organization’s actual risk. A critical flaw may have limited urgency when it is isolated by segmentation and access controls, while a medium-severity flaw may be more dangerous if it provides a route to credentials, privileged systems, or sensitive data. It presents attack-path validation as the process of determining whether weaknesses can be reached, exploited, combined, and used to advance toward a meaningful objective.

The article says periodic penetration tests can become outdated as cloud infrastructure, applications, identities, configurations, assets, and controls change. It distinguishes automated vulnerability scanners, which identify known weaknesses, from autonomous penetration testing, which it says can perform reconnaissance, test authorization logic, attempt exploitation, pivot through environments, and produce evidence of compromise. BreachLock promotes its Breach360 platform as a continuously scalable autonomous testing service and states that human security professionals should remain responsible for interpreting business risk, remediation priorities, regulatory obligations, and acceptable residual risk.

  • A critical vulnerability on an isolated system may not warrant immediate remediation if segmentation, identity controls, and other defenses prevent an attacker from using it to reach important assets.
  • The article distinguishes automated scanning from autonomous testing by framing scanners as tools that identify possible weaknesses, while autonomous penetration testing is intended to produce evidence that a compromise path works.
  • Retesting after remediation and whenever environments change can verify whether security controls still work, rather than assuming a past penetration-test report reflects the current environment.
  • The article says autonomous testing can take over continuous, repeatable technical testing at scale, but human professionals remain responsible for determining business impact, operational constraints, regulatory obligations, and acceptable residual risk.
Key Points
  • 01A vulnerability’s severity score does not by itself show whether an attacker can reach it, exploit it, combine it with other weaknesses, and reach a meaningful target.
  • 02The article says a medium-severity flaw in an internet-facing application can pose more actionable risk than a critical flaw on an isolated system protected by strong controls.
  • 03It argues that point-in-time penetration tests can quickly become outdated as cloud infrastructure, applications, identities, configurations, assets, controls, and vulnerabilities change.
  • 04According to the article, autonomous penetration testing goes beyond automated vulnerability scanning by performing reconnaissance, testing authentication and authorization logic, attempting exploitation, pivoting through environments, and validating attack paths.
  • 05BreachLock presents Breach360 as a platform that can continuously identify and validate exploitable attack paths, while human security professionals retain responsibility for business-risk and remediation decisions.

hash concept

High severity means a security issue is considered serious and should usually be fixed quickly.

hong-kong other
Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China often mentioned as a location in cyber or business reporting.
host reputation concept

hosted concept
Hosted means a service, website, or system is running on someone’s server so other people can access it.
Hotel Wi-Fi providers organization
Organizations that operate or supply wireless internet access for hotels and their guests.
hotfix concept
A hotfix is a targeted software update released to fix a specific problem, often urgently.
hotfixes concept
Hotfixes are small urgent software updates released to fix a specific problem, often a security issue or serious bug.

human operators concept
Human operators are people who monitor, control, or make decisions about a system instead of leaving everything fully automated.
human oversight concept
Human oversight means people review or supervise an automated system's actions so mistakes or abuse can be caught.
Hunt technique
Hunt means to proactively search systems and networks for signs of hidden threats or attacker activity.

Hunting, often called threat hunting, means proactively searching for signs of attackers or suspicious activity instead of waiting for alerts.
huntress organization

identities concept

identity controls concept
Identity controls are security measures that manage who users are and what they are allowed to access.

impersonate technique

impersonation technique
Impersonation is pretending to be someone or something trusted in order to deceive people or systems.

In the wild means a security flaw or attack is being used on real targets, not just tested in a lab.
in-the-wild exploitation concept
In-the-wild exploitation means attackers are using a flaw in real-world activity rather than only in testing or research.
in-the-wild probes technique
Real-world attempts to test whether publicly exposed systems are vulnerable.
inbox concept

Incident concept
A security incident is an event that may harm systems, data, or users and needs investigation or response.
Incident responders concept
Incident responders are specialists who investigate cyberattacks, contain damage, and help organizations recover safely.
incident response concept
Incident response is the process of investigating and handling a security problem after it is found.
incidents concept
Incidents are security events that may harm systems, data, users, or business operations and need investigation or response.
indicator concept
An indicator is a clue such as an IP address, file hash, domain, or email that may point to malicious activity.
indicators concept
Indicators are clues such as IP addresses, domains, file hashes, or behaviors that may point to malicious activity.

industry partners organization

initial access technique

initial-access credentials concept

insider threat-actor

intelligence agencies organization

intelligence collection concept
Intelligence collection is the process of gathering information about targets, threats, or situations for decision-making.

Intelligence sharing is the practice of exchanging threat information between teams, companies, or governments to help others defend themselves.
internal chats concept

internal databases concept

internet-facing concept
Internet-facing describes a system or service that can be reached directly from the public internet.

intrusion concept

intrusions concept

investigation concept
An investigation is the process of examining evidence to understand what happened.
invoice fraud technique

invoices concept
Invoices are bills requesting payment for goods or services, commonly abused in business email scams.
iOS product

IP addresses protocol

iran

Government, police, and legal bodies in Ireland that enforce laws and carry out official actions.

misuse concept

objective concept

patching concept

payloads concept

personal data concept

personal electronic device concept

personal information concept

personally identifiable information concept
